Salesforce shares closed at US$247.61 after a mixed run, and recent moves in AI and customer engagement software now put a sharper spotlight on whether that price is justified by the company's earnings power. For investors, the key issue is how much of Salesforce's recent history and future ambitions are already baked into today's multiple.

Salesforce has delivered a 26.6% return over the past 3 years, which raises the question of how much earnings strength the current valuation is already assuming.

The agreed US$5.66b purchase of Braze, along with new AI agent and data partnerships, can influence how investors think about future profit margins and the timing of cash flows tied to Salesforce's earnings base.

Your read on Salesforce is one view; the desks covering it have another. See what analysts think Salesforce's shares could be worth.

The stock's next move may depend on whether Salesforce's current earnings profile, and the growth implied in it, can justify the price you see today.

If you are comparing Salesforce with other AI focused software opportunities, a targeted screen of 38 AI small caps can provide a broader starting list for further research.

Is Salesforce Still Cheap on Earnings?

The P/E ratio is a useful lens for Salesforce because earnings are a key driver for how investors weigh large, mature software platforms. Salesforce trades on roughly 21.1x earnings, which is well below the Software industry average of about 32.7x and far under the peer group near 44.7x. For a business of this scale, that gap suggests the market is not paying the same headline premium as it does for many other software stocks.

The Fair Ratio model, which adjusts for Salesforce's size, margins, sector and risk profile, points to a higher P/E than the current 21.1x, so the stock screens as undervalued on this yardstick. Because the Braze deal adds a sizeable AI customer engagement asset into the mix, some investors may view that lower multiple as leaving headroom if the combined earnings base remains stable. To judge whether that discount is justified, you would want to weigh factors such as integration risk, future spending on AI agents and how usage based billing shapes long term profitability. When deciding whether to buy, sell, or hold a stock, investors often rely on analyst recommendations. Media reports about rating changes by these brokerage-firm-employed (or sell-side) analysts often influence a stock's price, but are they really important?

Before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage, let's see what these Wall Street heavyweights think about Salesforce (CRM).

Salesforce currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.68, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 53 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.68 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy.

Of the 53 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 36 are Strong Buy and two are Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 67.9% and 3.8% of all recommendations.

Brokerage Recommendation Trends for CRM
Broker Rating Breakdown Chart for CRM

Check price target & stock forecast for Salesforce here>>>

The ABR suggests buying Salesforce, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation.

Are you wondering why? The vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover often results in a strong positive bias of their analysts in rating it. Our research shows that for every "Strong Sell" recommendation, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations.

In other words, their interests aren't always aligned with retail investors, rarely indicating where the price of a stock could actually be heading. Therefore, the best use of this information could be validating your own research or an indicator that has proven to be highly successful in predicting a stock's price movement.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, which classifies stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), is a reliable indicator of a stock's near-term price performance. So, validating the Zacks Rank with ABR could go a long way in making a profitable investment decision.

Zacks Rank Should Not Be Confused With ABR

Although both Zacks Rank and ABR are displayed in a range of 1--5, they are different measures altogether.

Broker recommendations are the sole basis for calculating the ABR, which is typically displayed in decimals (such as 1.28). The Zacks Rank, on the other hand, is a quantitative model designed to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.

Salesforce (CRM) has been one of the most searched-for stocks on Zacks.com lately. So, you might want to look at some of the facts that could shape the stock's performance in the near term.

Over the past month, shares of this customer-management software developer have returned +9%, compared to the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -0.8% change. During this period, the Zacks Internet - Software industry, which Salesforce falls in, has lost 6.6%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?

While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.

Earnings Estimate Revisions

Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.

We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.

Salesforce is expected to post earnings of $3.43 per share for the current quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +5.5%. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed +0.1%.

The consensus earnings estimate of $16.72 for the current fiscal year indicates a year-over-year change of +33.6%. This estimate has remained unchanged over the last 30 days.

For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $16.03 indicates a change of -4.1% from what Salesforce is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has changed +0.9%.

Having a strong externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, offers a more conclusive picture of a stock's price direction in the near term, since it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. Due to the size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, Salesforce is rated Zacks Rank #2 (Buy).

title: Can Adobe Stock Jump 50%?

To gauge whether Adobe (ADBE) stock can jump 50%, look at a part of the company you may overlook: its faster-growing subscriptions for business professionals and consumers. In seven of the last ten calendar years, the stock rose 50% or more from one close to a later close in the same year. Yet the shares lost 27.0% over the past year, and you probably still think of Adobe as software for creative professionals. So how big are those subscriptions?

Business Professionals And Consumers Bring Adobe 29% Of Subscriptions

Adobe sold $1.91 billion of subscriptions to business professionals and consumers in fiscal Q3 2026, up 16% from a year earlier. That pace makes them the faster-growing group so far. Adobe's subscriptions for creative and marketing professionals were far larger at $4.65 billion, but grew 13%.

Adobe maintains a wide reach with business professionals and consumers. On the September 10, 2026 call, management said monthly active users in this group rose more than 25% from a year earlier to over 900 million. The company is also targeting the next generation of business professionals by making student spaces in Acrobat available globally.

Adobe Is Choosing When To Turn Users Into Subscribers

Adobe says it will decide when to try to turn free users into paying subscribers. Management said on the September 10 call that the company is routing part of its traffic to its freemium products, which are free to start, to win customers and deepen their usage. Adobe will then convert those users into recurring revenue at the right time. This strategy, management added, balances winning new customers with growing recurring revenue.

Analysts questioned that approach on the call. When one analyst noted that net new annual recurring revenue was down 36% to 37% from a year earlier, management cited the shift toward freemium products as one of the drivers. Adobe finished fiscal Q3 2026 with $22.16 billion in remaining performance obligations, which represent contracted revenue the company has yet to book. That figure was up 8% from a year earlier.

Trading at 14.0 times Adobe's last twelve months of earnings, against 22.9 for the S&P 500, the stock price appears to allow for little from those users. Adobe's faster-growing business and consumer subscriptions show reported sales are still rising, but they do not settle the analysts' questions about new recurring revenue. Management raised its fiscal 2026 revenue and earnings targets on the call, but it only reiterated its target of 10.2% growth in ending annual recurring revenue.
